title: Introduction to Testing Node.js Applications
learning_outcomes: Describe Why automated tests matter and explain how it relates to Introduction to Testing Node.js Applications.
Demonstrate Test levels in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Test isolation.

content.intro: Introduction to Testing Node.js Applications is part of testing and quality assurance. This lesson connects Why automated tests matter, Test levels, Test isolation to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: Tests make expected behavior repeatable and reveal regressions across functions, modules, APIs, and asynchronous work. Test both expected results and failure cases; ensure cleanup runs even when a test fails.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Tests make expected behavior repeatable and reveal regressions across functions, modules, APIs, and asynchronous work. Use the built-in test runner or a documented project tool, assert observable behavior, and isolate tests from real services.

items.title: Why automated tests matter
items.text: Tests should assert observable behavior and include failure cases. Deterministic inputs and cleanup are more valuable than depending on network state or exact timing.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Introduction to Testing Node.js Applications. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with Why automated tests matter; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.
Test one failure or boundary case for Test levels, then explain why the outcome is expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only private implementation details or depending on network state and timing that the test does not control.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Use deterministic fixtures, timeouts, dependency seams, and assertions on externally visible outcomes.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
